questions.q: In which order should you read an explain plan?
questions.explain: A plan is a tree. Leaves such as scans produce rows, and each parent (Sort, Limit, Join) consumes its children's rows. The top line is the last step, which returns the result.
options: Top to bottom: the first line runs first
From the most indented node outwards: inner nodes produce rows for the nodes above them
Bottom to top, ignoring indentation
Only the first line matters

questions.q: A plan shows Seq Scan on orders (actual rows=10 loops=1) with Rows Removed by Filter: 99990. What does it tell you?
questions.explain: The scan checked every row against the filter and threw almost all of them away. Work proportional to the table, for an answer of 10 rows, is the classic sign of a missing index.
options: The query deleted 99,990 rows
PostgreSQL read 100,000 rows to return 10: a selective condition with no usable index
The table has 10 rows
The index was used 10 times

questions.q: Why does a lookup in a B-tree index on 100,000 rows read only two or three index pages?
questions.explain: With hundreds of entries per page, one level narrows the search by a factor of hundreds. The depth grows with the logarithm of the row count, so even billions of rows need only a few levels.
options: Because the index is cached in JavaScript memory
Because each page holds hundreds of sorted keys, so the tree is very shallow and a lookup follows one page per level
Because B-trees store only the first 1,000 values
Because PostgreSQL reads the index backwards

questions.q: You have an index on (customer_id, placed_at). Which query can use it efficiently?
questions.explain: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then by the second within each first value. Conditions on a leftmost prefix (customer_id, or customer_id plus placed_at) use it; a condition on placed_at alone finds matches scattered through the whole index.
options: where placed_at >= '2026-02-01'
where customer_id = 42 and placed_at >= '2026-02-01'
where status = 'pending'
where total_kobo > 500000

questions.q: The query is where customer_id = $1 and placed_at >= $2 order by placed_at. Which index fits best?
questions.explain: Equality columns first, then the range or sort column. Inside the entries for one customer, the index is ordered by placed_at, so the range is one contiguous stretch and already sorted.
options: (placed_at, customer_id)
(customer_id, placed_at)
(placed_at) and (customer_id) as two separate indexes
No index: ranges cannot use indexes

questions.q: After adding an index on (customer_id, placed_at desc), the "My orders" plan loses its Sort node. Why does that matter with limit 5?
questions.explain: For a customer with 5,000 orders, a Sort must fetch all 5,000 first. An index in the right order lets the query stop after the first 5, so the cost no longer depends on how many orders the customer has.
options: It does not matter: sorting 10 rows is free
The Index Scan returns rows already in order, so the Limit stops after 5 rows instead of fetching and sorting all of the customer's orders
Without a Sort node, the results are not ordered
Sort nodes cannot be combined with Limit

questions.q: 90% of orders have status = 'paid'. There is an index on status, yet where status = 'paid' uses a Seq Scan. Why?
questions.explain: Indexes help selective conditions. The planner estimates the matching fraction from statistics and chooses the cheaper plan. For a rare value such as 'cancelled', the same index is used.
options: The index is broken and needs reindex
Text columns cannot use B-tree indexes
Fetching 90% of the rows through the index would jump between index and heap for almost every row; reading the table straight through is cheaper
The planner only uses indexes on integer columns

questions.q: After a nightly import doubled a table, a query's plan shows rows=120 estimated but actual rows=250000. What should you do first?
questions.explain: Estimates that far from reality mean the statistics are stale, and a plan built on them is probably wrong. Autovacuum analyzes eventually, but after a bulk load you run analyze yourself.
options: Add another index
Run analyze on the table so the planner has current statistics
Increase the server's memory
Rewrite the query as a subquery

questions.q: There is a B-tree index on placed_at. Which condition can use it?
questions.explain: Only the half-open range compares the bare column. The others compute something from the column for every row first, so the index on the column does not match; they would need an index on exactly that expression.
options: where placed_at::date = '2026-02-01'
where extract(month from placed_at) = 2
where placed_at >= '2026-02-01' and placed_at < '2026-02-02'
where to_char(placed_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD') = '2026-02-01'

questions.q: A unique index exists on lower(email). Which lookup uses it?
questions.explain: An expression index serves queries that use exactly the same expression. Write lookups the way the index is defined, or the planner falls back to a Seq Scan.
options: where email = $1
where lower(email) = lower($1)
where email ilike $1
where upper(email) = upper($1)

questions.q: An index is defined as on orders (placed_at) where status = 'pending'. When can the planner use it?
questions.explain: A partial index contains only the rows matching its condition. A query that might need other rows cannot use it, so the query must include that condition (or one that implies it).
options: For any query on placed_at
Only when the query's conditions imply status = 'pending'
Only for update statements
Only after vacuum

questions.q: Which rule does create unique index on carts (customer_id) where status = 'open' enforce?
questions.explain: Uniqueness applies only among the rows in the partial index, the open carts. It is also how you keep a value unique among non-deleted rows with soft deletes.
options: Every customer has exactly one cart
A customer has at most one open cart, but may have any number of checked-out carts
Carts cannot change status
Only one customer may have an open cart at a time

questions.q: What does include (total_kobo) add to an index on (customer_id)?
questions.explain: Included columns are payload, not part of the key: they do not affect sorting or searching, but they let the index "cover" the query without visiting the heap.
options: It sorts the index by total_kobo within each customer
It stores total_kobo in the leaf entries, so queries needing only customer_id and total_kobo can be answered by an index-only scan
It makes total_kobo unique per customer
It creates a second index on total_kobo

questions.q: An Index Only Scan shows Heap Fetches: 1440 for 1,440 rows. What is going on?
questions.explain: An index cannot tell whether a row is visible to your transaction. For pages the visibility map marks all-visible, the heap visit is skipped. Right after a bulk load nothing is marked yet; vacuum (or autovacuum) sets the bits.
options: The index is corrupt
The visibility map does not yet mark those pages as all-visible, so PostgreSQL had to check each row in the heap; vacuum fixes it
The query returned duplicate rows
The index does not contain the needed columns

questions.q: Which index does PostgreSQL not create automatically?
questions.explain: Primary keys and unique constraints need an index to work. A foreign key only needs one on the referenced side, which already has it. The referencing column, the one you join and delete through, is up to you.
options: The index behind a primary key
The index behind a unique constraint
An index on the referencing column of a foreign key, such as order_lines.order_id
None: PostgreSQL indexes every constrained column

questions.q: A table gets four extra indexes. What happens to inserts?
questions.explain: In the lesson, four indexes roughly tripled the WAL records for the same 20,000 rows, and the indexes were larger than the table. Every index is paid for on every write.
options: Nothing: indexes only affect reads
Every insert also updates four more B-trees and writes more WAL, so inserts get slower and the database grows
Inserts get faster because rows are found faster
Inserts are refused until the indexes are rebuilt

questions.q: Why can indexing a column like last_seen_at, updated on every request, slow down updates more than you expect?
questions.explain: Heap-only tuple (HOT) updates keep the new row version on the same page and skip every index. Changing an indexed column rules that out, so each update now writes to every index on the table.
options: Timestamps cannot be indexed
PostgreSQL can often update a row without touching any index (a HOT update), but only when no indexed column changes
It makes the table read-only
Each update rebuilds the whole index

questions.q: Why do migrations on big tables use create index concurrently?
questions.explain: The trade is time for availability. It cannot run inside a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an invalid index to drop and retry.
options: It builds the index faster
A plain create index blocks writes to the table until it finishes; concurrently builds it without blocking writes, more slowly
It creates the index on all replicas at once
It lets the index be created inside a transaction

questions.q: In pg_stat_statements, what is the difference between sorting by total_exec_time and by mean_exec_time?
questions.explain: A 2 ms query called ten million times a day can cost more than a 3-second report run once. Look at both lists: one for capacity, one for user-facing latency.
options: They always give the same order
Total finds what costs the database most overall (including cheap queries run millions of times); mean finds what makes single requests slow
Mean includes planning time, total does not
Total is in seconds, mean in milliseconds, otherwise identical

questions.q: In pg_stat_statements, select * from order_lines where order_id = $1 is cheap per call but has 2,000,000 calls a day, 50 per page view of the order list. What is the fix?
questions.explain: This is the N+1 query problem: one query for the list, then one per row. Each call may already use an index; the cost is the round trips. One set-based query replaces fifty.
options: An index on order_lines.order_id
A bigger connection pool
Fetch the lines for all orders on the page in one query, with a join or where order_id = any($1)
Cache each query result for one second

questions.q: A plan test runs against a test database with 12 orders, and it fails because the plan uses a Seq Scan although the index exists. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Reading one page is cheaper than reading an index page and then a heap page. The planner is right; the test data is unrealistic. Seed the test table with production-like volumes and distributions.
options: The index was not created
On a tiny table a Seq Scan really is the fastest plan; plan tests need data of realistic size and shape
Plan tests can never work
explain (format json) ignores indexes

questions.q: Which index type fits "find products whose jsonb attributes contain {"colour": "black"}"?
questions.explain: GIN indexes the elements inside composite values (jsonb keys and values, array elements, words in a document), which is what containment queries (@>) need. B-tree is for ordered scalar values.
options: B-tree
GIN
A partial B-tree on colour
Hash

questions.explain: The whole table fits on one page. Reading it directly is cheaper than reading an index page and then that same heap page, so the planner, correctly, ignores the index.
options:

Bitmap Heap Scan on orders

Index Only Scan using orders_customer_idx on orders

questions.explain: B-tree leaves are linked in both directions, so a single-column index can be read backwards for desc. The direction only matters in composite indexes with mixed orders, such as (customer_id, placed_at desc) for order by customer_id, placed_at desc.
options:
Limit

        ->  Seq Scan on orders

Limit

questions.explain: placed_at is the second column. Its values are spread through the sections of all 5,000 customers, so the index cannot find the range in one place. With so many distinct leading values, even PostgreSQL 18's skip scan is not worth it, and the planner reads the table.
options:
Aggregate

Aggregate

questions.explain: Each query that used an index adds one scan to it. Three customer lookups, one primary-key lookup, and nothing touched the total index, which makes it a candidate to drop.

orders_customer_idx=1 orders_pkey=1 orders_total_idx=0

questions.explain: The JSON plan is a tree: the Limit's Plans array holds the Index Scan. The index matches the filter and the sort order, so there is no Sort node.

questions.q: Two separate single-column indexes, and a condition with or. What is the top node of the plan?
questions.explain: Each index produces a bitmap of matching row locations, BitmapOr combines them, and the heap is read once. That is how PostgreSQL uses two single-column indexes for one or condition.
options:
Bitmap Heap Scan on orders
  ->  BitmapOr
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_coupon_idx
Seq Scan on orders
Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders

Append
  ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders
  ->  Index Scan using orders_coupon_idx on orders

questions.q: Estimate B-tree depth. Write levels(rows, perPage) returning how many levels a B-tree needs when each page holds perPage entries: one leaf level for up to perPage rows, and one more level each time the number of pages exceeds one page's worth.
questions.explain: Each level divides the number of pages by the fan-out. 100,000 rows need 200 leaf pages, which fit under one root: two levels. A billion rows need only four, which is why B-tree lookups stay fast as tables grow.

questions.q: Inside a leaf page, a B-tree finds the first key >= the search value by binary search. Write lowerBound(keys, value) returning that position (or keys.length if none), and use it to count how many keys fall in [from, to).
questions.explain: A range scan is two lower-bound searches and a walk between them: exactly what an Index Scan with placed_at >= $1 and placed_at < $2 does, across linked leaf pages.

questions.q: Write usableColumns(index, equalities, range): given an index's column list, the columns a query compares with =, and one optional range column, return how many leading index columns the search can use. Walk the index columns: equality columns continue the prefix; a range column is used and then stops it; anything else stops it.
questions.explain: With customer_id = and a placed_at range but no condition on status, only the first column narrows the search; placed_at is then checked entry by entry. That is why equality columns go first and the column order must match your queries.

questions.q: Write findSeqScans(planText) that returns, for each Seq Scan line in a text plan, the table name and the number from the following Rows Removed by Filter line (0 if there is none before the next node).
questions.explain: The orders scan removed 99,990 rows to keep 10: a missing index. The order_lines scan removed nothing because it kept every row for the hash join, which is a different problem: a missing index on the join column. Tools that parse plans for you (for example explain visualisers) do exactly this.

questions.q: pg_stat_statements groups queries that differ only in their constants. Write normalise(sql) that replaces each quoted string and each standalone number with $1, $2, … in order, then count calls per normalised query.
questions.explain: Grouping by shape, not by values, is what makes the statistics useful: a million lookups with different ids become one line with calls: 1000000. It is also why queries built by pasting values into text are harder to monitor, besides being unsafe.

questions.q: Make date filters sargable. Write dayRange(day) that turns "2026-02-28" into the half-open UTC range ["2026-02-28T00:00:00.000Z", "2026-03-01T00:00:00.000Z"], to be used as placed_at >= $1 and placed_at < $2.
questions.explain: Computing the bounds in the application keeps the column bare in SQL, so an index on placed_at serves the query. setUTCDate handles month and year ends; the upper bound is exclusive, so no timestamp is counted twice or missed.

questions.q: Imitate the planner's first decision. Write choosePlan(frequencies, value): look up the fraction of rows with that value (use 0.001 for values not in the table), and return "Seq Scan" when it is above 0.2, otherwise "Index Scan".
questions.explain: The real planner compares estimated costs rather than using a fixed threshold, and it also weighs how the rows are spread over pages. But the input is the same: the value's frequency from the statistics, which is why stale statistics lead to bad plans.
